source: Yeager et al. (2019) A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
finding: National Study of Learning Mindsets: a short online growth mindset course raised grades of lower-achieving ninth graders.
numbers: 65 US public schools, 12,490 students randomised individually. Lower achievers (n=6,320): +0.10 GPA points (95% CI 0.04-0.16, P=0.001), d=0.11. Pre-registered at osf.io/tn6g4.
limits: Average effect small; higher achievers showed no GPA gain (interaction B=0.09). Authors are the theory's proponents.
agent_relevance: Effect sizes of belief interventions on humans are about a tenth of a grade point. Do not expect a large lift from a belief-style prompt either.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) national experiment: intervention content and mindset manipulation check
finding: Two self-administered online sessions of about 25 minutes, about 20 days apart. Taught that abilities can be developed by effort, hard tasks, better strategies and help-seeking. Brain-as-muscle metaphor, older-student stories, reflection writing. Control taught brain function only.
numbers: Fixed-mindset score fell B=-0.38 on a 1-6 scale (95% CI -0.31 to -0.46), n=5,650, d=0.33, P<0.001. Three-item scale, e.g. 'You have a certain amount of intelligence, and you really can't do much to change it.'
limits: The belief change was large (d=0.33) but the grade change small (d=0.11): belief to behaviour transfer is leaky.
agent_relevance: Changing a stated belief is not the same as changing behaviour. Our schema should measure behaviour (checks passed), not stated attitude.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) national experiment: school-level moderators and Bayesian causal forest
finding: Effects depended on the school's peer norms for challenge seeking. Supportive norms gave larger gains. A blinded Bayesian causal forest confirmed the average effect and the moderator but shrank the estimates.
numbers: In low/medium-achieving schools with top-quartile norms, core GPA effect 0.18 points (third quartile 0.14); maths and science 0.16-0.25. Cross-school heterogeneity in GPA effect tau=0.09, Q=85.5, P=0.038; none in mindset change (Q=57.2, P=0.714). BCF posterior probability of a positive average effect at least 0.999.
limits: Norm measure was a worksheet task in each school's control group; several moderators tested.
agent_relevance: Same instruction, different context, different result. The effect of a motivational instruction should be tested per task type, not assumed.

source: Yeager et al. (2019) national experiment: advanced course-taking
finding: Intervention raised the chance of taking advanced maths (algebra II or higher) in tenth grade across the full cohort, an exploratory result.
numbers: +3 percentage points (95% CI 0.01-0.04), n=6,690, k=41 schools, P=0.001; 33% control to 36% treated, 9% relative increase.
limits: Exploratory outcome; only 41 schools had the data.
agent_relevance: Challenge seeking is the clean behavioural signature of the theory. For an agent, the analogue is choosing to attempt harder problems when allowed.

source: Blackwell, Trzesniewski & Dweck (2007) Implicit theories of intelligence predict achievement across an adolescent transition
finding: Study 1 followed seventh graders for two years: those who saw intelligence as malleable had rising maths grades, entity theorists flat grades. Study 2 taught malleability in an eight-session workshop and reversed the decline in maths grades.
numbers: Study 1 N=373. Study 2 experimental n=48 vs control n=43 (91 students). Read at abstract level.
limits: Full paper not opened. Small, in-person, multi-session, delivered by trained adults.
agent_relevance: Founding positive intervention. It needed several in-person sessions; a single prompt line is a much weaker dose.

source: Mueller & Dweck (1998) Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
finding: Six studies with fifth graders. Children praised for intelligence after success preferred performance goals, persisted less after failure, enjoyed tasks less, and performed worse than children praised for effort.
numbers: Six studies, fifth graders; cell sizes not read this session. Raw data for Studies 1 and 2 on osf.io/kgfhu (per Dweck & Yeager 2019).
limits: Abstract-level only. Replication evidence is mixed (see a11).
agent_relevance: Praise type changes later behaviour. For an LLM, feedback in a revision loop should name the process and the failing output (G2), not ability.

source: Dweck & Yeager (2019) Mindsets: A view from two eras
finding: Lineage: learned helplessness (Seligman & Maier 1967), attribution theory, Elliott & Dweck (1988) performance vs learning goals, Dweck & Leggett (1988) entity vs incremental theories. Mindsets are a meaning system tying goals, attributions, effort beliefs and helpless vs mastery responses.
numbers: Robins & Pals (2002): 363 Berkeley students over 3 years. Blackwell 2007 Study 1: 373 students over 2 years. Nationally representative 9th graders (over 14,000): fixed mindset vs GPA r=-.22.
quote: we still know far too little about how best to transmit a growth mindset to individuals
limits: Written by the theory's authors; paths are correlational. Dweck warns of 'false growth mindset': praise for effort alone, or posters with no changed practice.
agent_relevance: The meaning-system view is the useful formal piece: belief, then goal, then response to failure. Our schema encodes the response (G1 doubt on signal, G2 revise from output), not the belief.

source: Dweck & Yeager (2019): intervention era and sensitivity to materials
finding: Early in-person studies (Aronson 2002 college; Good 2003 and Blackwell 2007 adolescents) taught the brain-muscle metaphor. Online versions reached tens of thousands. Effects are modest, concentrated in lower achievers, about 0.10 GPA points, and depend on subtle features of materials. Economists replicated in Norway (Bettinger et al. 2018).
numbers: R&D: A/B tests about 3,000 participants, user testing about 300, head-to-head about 7,500. Largest adolescent field effects roughly 0.20 SD. Personality-mindset hot-sauce aggression study reduced retaliation.
limits: Yeager argues for education benchmarks (about 0.05-0.20 SD) instead of Cohen's lab cut points; critics disagree.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording is as fragile as intervention wording: tune on a dev set and expect it not to move to new tasks.

source: Hecht, Yeager & Dweck (2021) Beliefs, affordances, and adolescent development
finding: Mindset x Context framework: a belief helps only where the context affords acting on it. Contradicts the 'beliefs alone' hypothesis. Norway U-say trial: maths course-taking effect much stronger in districts with flexible tracks.
numbers: Norway RCT covered all but one of 50 high schools in the two largest counties (Rege et al. 2020). Chapter calls for interventions that guide teachers, not only students.
limits: Chapter, not a new trial; magnitudes of the Norway effect not extracted.
agent_relevance: An instruction only helps if the scaffold lets the agent act on it (retry budget, tools, checks). Motivation without affordance is inert.

source: Yeager, Dweck et al. (2021) What can be learned from growth mindset controversies?
finding: Large independent surveys show a mindset-achievement link; small samples sometimes find none. Authors argue heterogeneity, not absence, explains discrepancies.
numbers: California CORE N=300,629: r=.28 ELA, r=.27 maths. Three large studies (incl. NSLM, Norway U-say N=23,446) r=.24 with grades. Chile N=168,533 r=.34. PISA 2018 N=555,458, 74 nations: positive in 72 (exceptions China and Lebanon); single-item measure.
limits: Authors are proponents; correlational. Null associations: Czech applicants (Bahnik & Vranka 2017, N=5,653) and Chinese 5th-6th graders (Li & Bates 2019, N=433).
agent_relevance: Correlations of 0.2-0.3 between belief and score do not show that changing the belief changes the score.

source: Li & Bates (2019) mindset replication, as described by Yeager et al. (2021)
finding: Li & Bates found no significant mindset-grade correlation in 433 Chinese children and ran three experiments repeating Mueller & Dweck's praise study. One reached p<.05, one p<.10, each underpowered. Yeager et al. say that pooled, the three replicate at p<.05.
numbers: N=433 correlational sample; three praise experiments (cell sizes not read). Pooled p<.05 is the proponents' reading.
limits: Second-hand, from the theory's defenders; Li & Bates' own paper was not opened (not reachable).
agent_relevance: Even the founding praise effect is weak to marginal on replication. Treat motivational wording effects as fragile.

source: Sisk, Burgoyne, Sun, Butler & Macnamara (2018) Two meta-analyses of growth mind-sets
finding: Mindset-achievement links and intervention effects are both weak overall. Some benefit for low-SES or at-risk students.
numbers: Meta-analysis 1: k=273, N=365,915. Meta-analysis 2 (interventions): k=43, N=57,155. Overall effects weak (abstract; exact r and d not read).
limits: Abstract-level read. Yeager and colleagues dispute averaging over heterogeneous effects.
agent_relevance: Baseline expectation for any mindset-style scaffold: near zero on average, with pockets of benefit.

source: Burnette, O'Boyle, VanEpps, Pollack & Finkel (2013) Mind-sets matter: meta-analysis
finding: Incremental beliefs predict more learning goals, fewer performance goals, more mastery strategies, fewer helpless strategies, less negative affect. Effects stronger under ego threat.
numbers: k=113, unique N=28,217. Learning goals r=.187; performance goals r=-.151; helpless strategies r=-.238; mastery strategies r=.227; negative emotion r=-.233; expectations r=.157.
limits: Correlational; Macnamara & Burgoyne argue such estimates are inflated by bias.
agent_relevance: Mindset shows mainly in the response to threat (failure feedback). That maps to our failure-signal states.

source: Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023) Do growth mindset interventions impact academic achievement?
finding: Intervention meta-analysis: small average effect that is not significant after bias correction, near zero in the best studies. Authors with a financial interest reported larger effects.
numbers: All: 63 studies, N=97,672, d=0.05 (95% CI 0.02-0.09). Mindset actually changed: 13 studies, N=18,355, d=0.04 (-0.01 to 0.10). Highest quality: 6 studies, N=13,571, d=0.02 (-0.06 to 0.10).
limits: Abstract-level. Contested (see a15).
agent_relevance: The skeptic case. If the best-designed human trials show d about 0.02-0.10, belief-style instructions are a weak lever.

source: Yeager et al. commentary on Macnamara & Burgoyne and Burnette et al. (PMC10495100)
finding: Commentary argues the average hides heterogeneity. Re-analysing 122 effect sizes with multilevel models gives a larger mean and wide prediction intervals, and notes coding errors in the original.
numbers: Re-analysis: mean 0.09 SD (p<.001); tau2+omega2=0.16; prediction interval -0.22 to 0.40; at-risk 0.15 SD. After corrections: overall 0.05 (p=.004), at-risk 0.12 (p=.01). M&B prediction interval -0.09 to 0.19. Burnette et al.: overall 0.09, at-risk 0.16, interval -0.08 to 0.35. NSLM lower achievers about 0.11 SD; supportive contexts 0.15-0.20; Peru high-poverty 0.23-0.35.
limits: Written by NSLM authors; first 100,000 characters read. Dispute unresolved.
agent_relevance: Report the full distribution of effects, not the mean. We should show prompt effects as spread over tasks and seeds.

source: Bryan, Tipton & Yeager (2021) Behavioural science is unlikely to change the world without a heterogeneity revolution
finding: Average effects mislead when effects vary by person and context. Recommends large probability samples, measured moderators, pre-registered moderator plans.
numbers: Opower: initial 2% energy reduction in 17 field experiments, about 600,000 households; scale-up to about 8 million households gave a markedly smaller average. Hypothetical ATE roughly 0.07 SD that still works for more than half the population.
limits: Perspective article, no new growth-mindset data. First 100,000 characters read.
agent_relevance: Evaluate prompts by subgroup (task type, model size), not one pooled score.

source: Neural replication of Moser et al. (2011) mindset and error monitoring (PMC8318296)
finding: Tried to replicate the report that growth-minded adults show a smaller Pe (error-awareness brain signal). Did not replicate.
numbers: N=89 (planned minimum 65). Mindset x condition on uncorrected Pe F(1,87)=4.19, p=.044, wrong direction; after overlap correction F=2.51, p=.117. Mindset vs post-error accuracy r=.04, p=.697. Post-error slowing present: F(1,88)=8.84, p=.004.
limits: Single lab, student sample; authors say they 'could evidently not replicate'.
agent_relevance: No neural support that mindset changes error monitoring; error handling is better done by code-side checks.

source: Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999) Meta-analysis of extrinsic rewards and intrinsic motivation
finding: Tangible, expected rewards reduce later free-choice intrinsic motivation; positive verbal feedback raises it. Support for self-determination theory.
numbers: 128 studies. Free-choice d: engagement-contingent -0.40, completion-contingent -0.36, performance-contingent -0.28. Self-reported interest d=-0.15 and -0.17. Positive feedback d=+0.33 (free choice), +0.31 (interest). Tangible rewards worse for children.
limits: Abstract-level; disputed by other meta-analyses (not read).
agent_relevance: Rewards shift behaviour from the task to the reward. Relevant to RL on verifiable rewards: reward hacking is the machine overjustification.

source: Yin, Wang, Horio, Kawahara & Sekine (2024) Should we respect LLMs? Prompt politeness across languages
finding: Eight politeness levels in English, Chinese and Japanese on summarisation, MMLU-style benchmarks and bias detection. Rude prompts often hurt; very polite ones do not help; best level differs by language.
numbers: English GPT-3.5 best at level 8 (60.02), level 3 close (59.44), level 1 gives 51.93, significantly lower. Llama2-70B scores rise roughly with politeness. GPT-4 stable. Chinese GPT-3.5: level 8 low, level 1 lowest. GPT-4 lowest bias at level 6.
limits: Small differences between neighbouring levels; strong models show little sensitivity; models are old (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama2).
agent_relevance: Tone matters little for strong models. Keep prompts neutral and plain; do not spend schema budget on flattery or threats.

source: Li et al. (2023) Large language models understand and can be enhanced by emotional stimuli (EmotionPrompt)
finding: Appending emotional sentences such as 'This is very important to my career' raised scores across 45 tasks and 6 models, with a human study on generative tasks.
numbers: 8.00% relative gain on Instruction Induction, 115% on BIG-Bench; human study 106 participants, 10.9% average gain in performance, truthfulness and responsibility. Models: Flan-T5-Large, Vicuna, Llama 2, BLOOM, ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613), GPT-4. Temperature 0.7.
limits: BIG-Bench 115% is a relative change from low base accuracies; gains larger at high temperature (so partly noise reduction).
agent_relevance: The one LLM motivation result with a measured effect, but it depends on base accuracy. Test against our G1 and variance controls before use.

source: Li et al. (2023) EmotionPrompt: stimuli list and ablations
finding: Eleven stimuli from three psychological theories: self-monitoring (EP01-03, e.g. 'You'd better be sure.'), social cognitive theory (EP04-06), cognitive emotion regulation (EP07-11, incl. 'Embrace challenges as opportunities for growth', a growth-mindset-style line). EP02 best on Instruction Induction, EP06 on BIG-Bench; best beats worst by 6.06% on Instruction Induction.
numbers: Gain larger for larger models (notably Vicuna and Llama 2); larger in few-shot than zero-shot; relative gain grows with temperature; EmotionPrompt curves flatter across temperature than vanilla. Attention analysis on Flan-T5-large: emotional words get larger input attention weights.
limits: Best stimulus differs by benchmark, so the best line is unstable. Attention story is correlational.
agent_relevance: Growth-mindset-flavoured lines are among the stimuli with no clean separation from other lines. No evidence of a distinct mindset mechanism in LLMs.

source: Yang et al. (2023) Large language models as optimizers (OPRO), 'Take a deep breath'
finding: Automatic prompt search found 'Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step.' gave the top zero-shot GSM8K accuracy for PaLM 2-L, ahead of 'Let's think step by step.'
numbers: GSM8K: 80.2 vs 71.8 for Kojima's prompt vs 34.0 with an empty instruction.
limits: A search-found phrase tuned on a training split; the paper claims no psychological mechanism.
agent_relevance: Wording gains are real but search-found and model-specific. Do not import them as a schema rule; tune per model on held-out items (G3).

source: Bsharat, Myrzakhan & Shen (2023) Principled instructions are all you need (26 principles incl. tip)
finding: 26 prompt principles tested on LLaMA-1/2 and GPT-3.5/4; principle 10 adds 'I'm going to tip $xxx for a better solution!'. Gains are reported for the set overall.
numbers: On GPT-4, average quality +57.7% and correctness +36.4% across principles (set as a whole, not tip alone). Absolute accuracy 20-40% on average, above 40% for large models.
limits: Authors' own small question set; the tip principle is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Incentive lines (tips, career importance) are the LLM version of extrinsic reward. Evidence per line is thin; we skip them.

source: Dweck & Leggett (1988) A social-cognitive approach to motivation and personality (Psychological Review 95, 256-273)
finding: Founding theory, known only through Dweck & Yeager 2019: implicit theories of ability (entity vs incremental) lead to performance or learning goals, then to helpless or mastery-oriented patterns after failure.
numbers: No numbers recorded from the paper itself.
limits: Not opened (paywalled). Pointer only.
agent_relevance: A three-link chain: belief, goal, response to failure. Our schema carries only the last link.

source: Ryan & Deci (2000) Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation
finding: SDT: three basic needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness); controlling contexts undermine intrinsic motivation, competence-affording feedback supports it. Paper not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Competence feedback helps; the schema's check results play that role (informative, not controlling).

source: Bandura (1977) Self-efficacy: toward a unifying theory of behavioral change
finding: Self-efficacy forms from mastery experience, vicarious experience, persuasion and arousal, and predicts effort and persistence. Pointer only; not opened.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, mastery experience maps to solved in-context examples and passed checks rather than encouragement.

source: Rege et al. (2020) U-say Norway RCT, as described in Hecht et al. (2021) and Yeager et al. (2021)
finding: Randomised trial in nearly all high schools of two Norwegian counties; the intervention changed maths course choices, much more where tracks were flexible.
numbers: About 49 of 50 schools; N=23,446 in the survey subset with r=.24 mindset-grade association (pooled with other large studies in Yeager et al. 2021).
limits: Second-hand description; primary paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Structural affordance decides whether a belief change shows up. Same lesson as a09.
